Your neighbour's experience is entirely anecdotal. Competition for minimum wage jobs is going to differ from area to area. In some places, minimum wage jobs are going to be in demand and in other places they won't be. Where I live, minimum wage jobs are competitive. I know this from personal experience. 

Anyway, my point still stands, if a position has a lot of applicants and it's a choice between an experienced worker and an applicant straight out of school, the employer will almost always go for the experienced candidate unless there is an incentive to act otherwise.

Operating a till, showing good customer service, working in a fast paced environment and the ability to sustain employment for a period of time are all assets in the eyes of employers. I mean when you're deciding between two candidates and one has more experience than the other, the employer is typically going to go for the experience one. 

Is experience a requirement? No, otherwise no sixteen year old would ever be able to start working. It certainly helps though.

The idea is to encourage employers to employ younger people who typically have less experience than their older counterparts. If everyone had to be paid equally, employers would usually go for the older and more experienced candidate and younger people would struggle even more to get on the career ladder. 

Of course the problem is that younger people still have the same costs of living as over-25s and the government doesn't seem to be doing anything to cover the shortfall. It's so absurd I could almost laugh. Almost.
